intro: These living and historical art traditions come from different communities. The comparison focuses on how a line can connect, describe or transform a figure.
alt: Microsoft sees a formline study, horses on ledger paper, an Inuit print study and a brightly outlined Woodlands-influenced fish study.

variants.name: Northwest Coast formline
variants.look: Follow the thick line around the bent inner shapes and smaller colored areas.
variants.history: The term formline describes design principles used in a number of Northwest Coast art traditions. Haida artists and artists of other nations use distinct repertoires and conventions.
variants.when: Study attributed public examples to understand how a line's thickness guides the eye between connected forms.
variants.why: Changing line weight helps neighboring shapes read as part of the same design.

variants.name: Plains ledger art
variants.look: The horses and riders are built from flat outline shapes, with the ledger's ruling still visible.
variants.history: From the nineteenth century, many Plains artists made narrative drawings on ledger paper as one of several available surfaces. Artists continue the practice today.
variants.when: Study the position and detail of a figure as a way to tell an event in a small space.
variants.why: Selective detail keeps the focus on the actors and movements that matter to the story.

source.label: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

variants.name: Kinngait print
variants.look: The open paper makes the strong animal silhouette and small patches of blue easy to read.
variants.history: Inuit artists and printmakers in Kinngait, Nunavut, developed a print studio practice in the late 1950s and continue to publish and innovate.
variants.when: Study a documented edition to see how drawing and printmaking can be collaborative steps.
variants.why: A print's contours and areas of color convey the decisions of both the designer and the person making the edition.

variants.name: Woodlands School
variants.look: A strong outline holds the fish shape together, while interior lines link small colored sections.
variants.history: Anishinaabe artist Norval Morrisseau helped establish a modern school of painting in Canada. Many artists developed distinct work through it.
variants.when: Study an original artist's work to see how internal and connecting lines express relationships inside a picture.
variants.why: A clear outer silhouette can coexist with complex interior relationships.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. She is a visiting museumgoer, visibly present in a corner of each frame. Artwork gets most of the visual space. Scene list in exact order: Northwest Coast formline contemporary public study, bold black flowing lines building red and black ovoid and U-shape figures, on a clean mounted study surface; Plains ledger art facsimile as a page of ruled ledger paper with original modern study of horses in thin outline and flat wash, no readable writing; Kinngait print study use clean reduction-like black and blue animal silhouettes and paper, contemporary original motif; Woodlands School print study, outlined fish with colored interior line structure, contemporary illustration techniques on clean mount. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
